open-question.question: An open_questions.xml written before this change keeps the recommendation last until some subcommand next writes it, and sort writes nothing when no block moves. Is that lazy conversion on the next write enough, or should some write path (for example sort, or every read) convert an old-order document right away?
open-question.alternative: Change nothing beyond the renderer: an old-order document keeps its recommendation last until one of the existing writers (add, strip that changes something, embed, remove, or a sort that moves a block) next saves it, and the reordering happens then. It adds no code, no subcommand, and no new write condition. Read-only subcommands (list, locate, lift, walk) stay non-writing, and sort keeps its "writes only when a block moved" rule. In practice the gap closes quickly, since any embed or answer on the milestone rewrites the whole file. Until that next write, the file's bytes and the tool's canonical rendering differ. `cmd_locate` prints `_question_lines` on the stated assumption that the file always holds the serializer's own output, so its print (which callers use as commit bodies) can disagree with the file in the meantime. The first unrelated write then also carries a reorder diff for every recommendation-bearing block, mixed into a commit about something else, such as one answer.

Widen `cmd_sort`'s write condition from "a block moved" to "the canonical rendering differs from the file's current bytes". That way the sort step that ends every recommendation pass also converts an old-order document, in its own separately committed reorder. The conversion happens at a predictable point, on a subcommand whose job is already "put the document in canonical order". It lands in the dedicated sort commit behind the dirty-path guard instead of inside an answer or embed commit. Read-only subcommands stay non-writing. It changes sort's documented contract, which today orders blocks only and writes only when one moves, and the goal restates that sort keeps ordering blocks only. It needs a byte comparison against the file plus new tests. It also only helps once someone runs a recommendation pass or sort, so a document that skips sort still converts lazily.

Have `load_document` (or every subcommand, reads included) rewrite the file in canonical form whenever it is not already, so any tool call, even list, locate, lift, or walk, converts an old-order document immediately. It closes the gap completely and at once. After any tool call the file is exactly the serializer's output, so `cmd_locate`'s "file holds canonical lines" assumption holds for every print. It turns read-only subcommands into writers. Read-only agents, read-only Q&A, and the answer sweep's lift-as-skip then dirty `open_questions.xml` as a side effect no skill commits. That can trip the dirty-own-path guard or ride into an unrelated commit, and it breaks the tool's split between reads and writes.

Leave all existing subcommands as they are and give the maintainer or user an explicit conversion path, such as a small `normalize` subcommand or a documented no-op-style rewrite. They run it once against an old-order document and commit the result on its own. The conversion is deliberate, visible, and isolated in its own commit. No existing subcommand's write condition or read-only guarantee changes. It adds a subcommand or procedure used essentially once per document, which amounts to migration scaffolding. The project deliberately avoids migrations (pre-split milestones get none), and nothing ensures anyone actually runs it. Old-order documents that nobody converts fall back to lazy conversion anyway.
open-question.recommendation: Every existing document holding blocks is this milestone's own, which is emptied before the change can land, and the project records no migrations; the goal already makes the reorder a property of every write and says sort keeps ordering blocks only, so widening sort, rewriting on read, or a one-shot subcommand would each add a contract change for a document that in practice never exists.

open-question.question: The recommend-all-open-questions skill, docs/skill-reference.md, docs/workflow.md, and the CLAUDE.md invariants say the recommendation pass and embed --recommendation leave a block's <alternative> children untouched. Once embedding a recommendation moves the named alternative to the front, should that claim change to "alternatives' content and set unchanged, their order the renderer's", or be dropped wherever it appears?
open-question.alternative: At every site that makes the claim, replace "untouched" with the question's proposed wording: the alternatives' content and set are unchanged, and their order is the renderer's. The sites are recommend-all-open-questions SKILL.md line 25 ("never touches a block's `<alternative>` children") and line 212, the embed --recommendation passage in docs/skill-reference.md, the matching passage in docs/workflow.md, and the CLAUDE.md invariant. Each site stays accurate and complete. A reader who sees the recommended alternative jump to the front in the Recommendation-annotation commit diff finds the move explained where the guarantee is stated, instead of reading it as the pass breaking its own contract. The renderer's ordering rule then appears as a clause in skill prose and docs, while the tool's canonical-form docstring is already its single home. CLAUDE.md says runtime prose states the tool's contract in at most one sentence per site and never restates rendering mechanics, and every extra mention is one more place that must change if the ordering rule changes later.

Replace "untouched" with the "frozen set" wording the skill and the tool already use elsewhere (SKILL.md lines 11, 66, 100, 114 and 131, and the tool's embed and strip help). Each site would then say the pass never adds, drops, or edits an alternative, and none of them would mention order. Where the order is stated at all, it is stated once, in the tool's module docstring and `--help` canonical-form contract, which this milestone rewrites anyway. It keeps the real guarantee the recommendation half needs, that the option set it picks from never changes. It matches vocabulary the files already use, and it leaves child order to the tool, so no prose site needs another edit if the ordering rule changes. A reader of the skill or the docs alone gets no warning that embedding a recommendation reorders alternatives, and has to reach the tool's help to learn why the diff shows a moved `<alternative>`. The capture skill reads the alternatives "in document order" as "the options the user saw", and that reading needs its own separate fix either way.

Delete the untouched-alternatives claim from every site that makes it and add nothing in its place. The fragment checks the tool already makes (no `<alternative>` in a recommendation fragment, exactly one `<recommendation>` naming one of the block's own ids) are left to stand as the only statement of what the pass can and cannot change. It is the smallest edit, and it removes a claim the new renderer makes literally false without writing a replacement contract that could drift from the tool. It throws away a guarantee that is still true and matters: the recommendation pass never changes the option set. The enumerate-versus-pick split recorded in CLAUDE.md depends on that set staying frozen, and once the statement is gone a later editor has no written rule stopping them from letting the pick pass rewrite or prune alternatives.
open-question.recommendation: The guarantee the enumerate-versus-pick split actually needs is that the pass never adds, drops, or edits an alternative, which is the frozen-set wording these files already use; child order is the tool's by the standing invariant, so stating it once in the tool's canonical-form contract neither restates rendering mechanics at five prose sites nor leaves the frozen set unguarded as dropping the claim would.
